newsitem.title: USA: Parties clash over future of Speaker Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Parties clash over future of Speaker Gingrich.

text.p: A House Republican leader said on Sunday that despite pending ethics violation action against House Speaker Newt Gingrich, support for his re-election remained strong.
"We have seen no erosion whatesoever," House Majority Whip Tom DeLay, a Texas Republican, said on NBC's "Meet the Press," and he predicted Gingrich's re-election on Jan. 7.
But Representative Martin Frost, a Texas Democratic appearing on the same show, saw it differently, forecasting Gingrich's ultimate resignation.

"When all is said and done," said Frost, chairman of his party's Congressional Campaign Committee, Republicans will demand that ethical standards be upheld "and Newt eventually, on his own, will step down and there will be a new speaker."
Frost called for a public hearing by the House Ethics Committee on a penalty for Gingrich, but said it should not be rushed and held just ahead of the House vote.
He said all the evidence should be presented and Gingrich, a Georgia Repubican who has been a lightning rod for House Democrats, be given a chance to reply.
DeLay said he hoped the panel could meet before the vote, had no problem with a public hearing and was sure Gingrich would appear before it, if asked.
Gingrich was cited by the panel for using money from a tax-exempt charitable organisation to finance a college course that was broadcast to conservative gatherings.

The speaker has admitted he violated House rules and that in failing to get legal advice that would have steered him away from use of a tax-exempt foundation his conduct did not reflect creditably on the House.
The ethics panel will decide on Gingrich's punishment, which could could range from a reprimand to expulsion.
Representative John Linder, a Georgia Republican, said on "Fox News Sunday" that "We want public hearings, too. We'd like them Thursday or Friday."

Ethics Committee chairman Nancy Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, said in an interview with the Washington Post that she wanted an early and public decision on the penalities, and hoped to have a timetable set by Monday.
Some Democrats have called for Gingrich to step down, but others are said to prefer he stay on grounds it would be easier for President Bill Clinton to deal with a weak speaker.
Linder said: "They want to keep this in the public eye as long as Clinton is being accused of laundering money," a reference to allegations that Democrats had accepted illegal campaign contributions.
Frost said: "This is a matter of the integrity of the House" and that the standards that were applied to former Speaker Jim Wright should be applied to Gingrich.
In 1989, Gingrich helped to bring down Wright as House Speaker on ethics charges. The Texan resigned voluntarily.
Wright, on the ABC programme "This Week," had no advice for Gingrich, but said that while he himself had done nothing wrong, the charges against him were polarising Congress.
Asked what Gingrich should do, Wright said "he will have to examine his own conscience."
